target_property_anchors.text: 1.1 Write $r=\sqrt3$. Direct addition gives $\sum h_j=8/(4\sqrt2)=\sqrt2$. The numerator of $\sum g_j$ is $(1-r)-(3-r)+(3+r)-(1+r)=0$, and the numerator of $\sum jg_j$ is $-(3-r)+2(3+r)-3(1+r)=0$. Thus $g$ has the required zero sum and two vanishing moments. 1.2 With denominator $32$, the numerator of $\sum h_j^2$ is $(4+2r)+(12+6r)+(12-6r)+(4-2r)=32$, so the zero-shift autocorrelation is $1$. The only possible nonzero even-shift autocorrelation of a four-tap filter is at shift $2$ or $-2$; at shift $2$ its numerator is $(3-r)(1+r)+(1-r)(3+r)=2r-2r=0$, and the shift $-2$ sum is the same by reindexing. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Ω\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. If
$u\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$$D_i u=0\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega\qquad(1\le i\le n),$$
then for every connected component $C$ of $\Omega$ there is a constant
$c_C\in\mathbb K$ such that $u=c_C$ almost everywhere on $C$. The empty
domain has no components, so its conclusion is vacuous.

The proof assumes full AC as stated, but uses it only through Countable Choice
for the Sobolev representative, Lebesgue, and mollification interfaces cited
below. No full-AC selection is made in the ball propagation argument.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

candidates.target_interface:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume AC, including its CC and DC consequences. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron and let $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ be a shape-regular family of matching affine tetrahedral meshes with $h=\max_K\operatorname{diam}K\to0$. Set $V_h=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $S_h=W_h^0\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$, and define
$$X_h=\{v_h\in V_h:(v_h,\nabla q_h)_{L^2}=0\text{ for every }q_h\in S_h\}.$$
Every sequence $v_h\in X_h$ bounded in $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$. Moreover there is $C$ independent of $h$ such that $\|v_h\|_2\le C\|\operatorname{curl}v_h\|_2$ for all $v_h\in X_h$.

The precise harmonic-quotient version is as follows. On any bounded Lipschitz polyhedron for which the regular decomposition and relative commuting projections below are proved, put $K=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{H_0(\operatorname{curl})})$, $K_h=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{V_h})$ and
$$\mathcal H=K\cap(\nabla H_0^1)^\perp,\qquad\mathcal H_h=K_h\cap(\nabla S_h)^\perp.$$
Both harmonic spaces are finite dimensional. Discrete compactness still holds on $X_h$, while the uniform curl Poincare inequality holds on $Z_h=V_h\cap K_h^\perp=X_h\cap\mathcal H_h^\perp$. A nonzero vector of $\mathcal H_h$ prevents that inequality on all of $X_h$. These are the harmonic spaces of the relative boundary complex; the full-space absolute cohomology dimensions do not identify them.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron and let $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ be a shape-regular family of matching affine tetrahedral meshes with $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}(K)\to0$. For the full lowest-order spaces $E_h^0=W_h^0,E_h^1=N_h^1,E_h^2=N_h^2,E_h^3=N_h^3$ of [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]], there are linear projections $\pi_h^k:L^2\Lambda^k(\Omega)\to E_h^k$ satisfying $\pi_h^k|_{E_h^k}=I$ and $d\pi_h^k=\pi_h^{k+1}d$ on $H\Lambda^k(\Omega)$ for $k=0,1,2$. In degree three the exterior derivative is zero. Their norms are uniformly bounded both in $L^2$ and in $H\Lambda^k$, for $k=0,1,2,3$.

There is also a boundary-corrected family of projections $\pi_{h,0}^k:L^2\Lambda^k(\Omega)\to E_{h,0}^k$, where $E_{h,0}^k=E_h^k\cap H_0\Lambda^k(\Omega)$ and $H_0\Lambda^k$ is the graph closure of compactly supported smooth forms. These have the same uniform bounds, are the identity on $E_{h,0}^k$, and commute in degrees zero through two on the homogeneous complex; the terminal degree-three differential is zero. In particular,
$$\pi_{h,0}^0:H_0^1(\Omega)\to W_h^0\cap H_0^1(\Omega),\qquad \pi_{h,0}^1:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega),\qquad \nabla\pi_{h,0}^0=\pi_{h,0}^1\nabla.$$
Here the zero tangential space uses [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Each family converges strongly in $L^2$ on every $L^2$ form, uniformly on compact $L^2$ subsets, and in the graph norm on its corresponding graph domain. candidates.target_interface:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz domain, let $d\ge1$, and fix constants $\varepsilon>0$, $M>0$, and $\kappa>0$. Put
$$F_\varepsilon(s)=\frac{(s^2-1)^2}{4\varepsilon^2},\qquad f_\varepsilon(s)=F_\varepsilon'(s)=\frac{s^3-s}{\varepsilon^2},$$
and define the free energy on $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)\cap L^4(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ by
$$\mathcal E_\varepsilon(u)=\int_\Omega\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}|\nabla u|^2+F_\varepsilon(u)\right)\,dx.$$
Here $H^1=W^{1,2}$ and weak derivatives have the meaning in [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The finite-energy initial class consists of $u_0\in H^1(\Omega)\cap L^4(\Omega)$.

The **Allen–Cahn gradient flow** is
$$u_t=-M\mu,\qquad \mu=-\kappa\Delta u+f_\varepsilon(u),\qquad \partial_nu=0,\qquad u(0)=u_0.$$
The **Cahn–Hilliard gradient flow** is
$$u_t=M\Delta\mu,\qquad \mu=-\kappa\Delta u+f_\varepsilon(u),\qquad \partial_nu=\partial_n\mu=0,\qquad u(0)=u_0.$$
For weak solutions, the no-flux conditions are encoded by the natural weak formulations with all $H^1(\Omega)$ test functions. In dimensions $d\ge5$, the finite-energy class $H^1\cap L^4$ alone does not in general make $f_\varepsilon(u)$ a continuous functional on $H^1(\Omega)$: it gives only $f_\varepsilon(u)\in L^{4/3}$, while $H^1(\Omega)$ need not embed into $L^4(\Omega)$. Thus any weak solution tested against all $H^1$ functions must have the additional integrability needed to make the nonlinear pairing continuous. The chemical potential $\mu$ is the variational derivative of $\mathcal E_\varepsilon$, and the mobilities select the $L^2$ metric for Allen–Cahn and the mean-zero $H^{-1}$ metric for Cahn–Hilliard. In the Cahn–Hilliard flow, the no-flux equation conserves $\int_\Omega u$; the Allen–Cahn flow has no such conservation law in general. No maximum-principle property is part of these definitions.

The convergence theorem on this page is restricted to one space dimension. Assuming the Axiom of Choice for the following standard embedding consequences, if $d=2$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded $W^{1,p}$ extension domain for every $1<p<2$ as defined in [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]], then [[thm-critical-sobolev-embedding-into-every-finite-lq]] gives $H^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^4(\Omega)$. If $d=3$ and $\Omega$ is a bounded $W^{1,2}$ extension domain, then [[thm-sobolev-embedding-on-bounded-extension-domains-for-p-less-than-n]] gives $H^1(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^4(\Omega)$. These are the exact extra extension hypotheses for the quartic-energy claim. In dimensions $d\ge4$ no assertion that every $H^1$ state has finite quartic energy is made; the explicit initial class above remains $H^1\cap L^4$. No sharp-interface limit as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ is part of either definition.
